metadata.title: LEGAL ISSUES IN THE USE OF DIGITAL EVIDENCE IN JUDICIAL PROCEEDINGS AND THE DIFFERENTIATION OF CRIMINAL LIABILITY
metadata.description: This study examines the legal and procedural use of digital evidence in criminal proceedings and its significance for the differentiation and individualization of criminal liability. The research employs comparative legal, formal legal, systemic, and analytical methods, with reference to the legislation of Uzbekistan, the Budapest Convention, and selected practices of the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Estonia, and the Republic of Korea. The findings reveal persistent problems concerning the legal status, admissibility, authentication, preservation, chain of custody, technical examination, and cross-border acquisition of digital evidence, as well as deficiencies in institutional capacity and professional expertise. The study establishes that reliable digital evidence is essential for determining the method of commission, form of guilt, role of participants, extent of harm, and transnational character of offences. It concludes that uniform procedural standards, stronger forensic institutions, specialized training, scientifically grounded liability criteria, and enhanced international cooperation are necessary.
keywords: digital evidence, criminal proceedings, digital forensics, admissibility of evidence, chain of custody, criminal liability, individualization of punishment, international cooperation.

metadata.description:
Dominant Regulatory Axis Detection (DRA): A Mechanistic, Low‑Dimensional Approach for Identifying Major Transcriptional Shifts in Clinical RNA‑seq and Single‑Cell Studies

Abstract

Dominant Regulatory Axis (DRA) is a lightweight, mechanistically grounded method for identifying the strongest transcriptional regulatory shift between two biological or clinical states. Instead of producing long, diffuse pathway lists, DRA isolates the top magnitude‑of‑change genes and maps them to compact transcription factor signatures, yielding interpretable axis scores such as NFκB, p53, or NR3C1. The method is robust to cohort heterogeneity, simple to deploy, and suitable for clinical‑trial pipelines. This deposit includes a reference implementation, minimal TF signatures, example data, documentation, provenance, and an optional integration provision for GeneXplain.

Description

Background

Relapse biology in acute myeloid leukemia and other clinical contexts often converges on a small number of dominant transcriptional axes rather than broad, evenly distributed pathway changes. DRA operationalizes this observation by ranking genes by magnitude of change between two states and mapping the strongest changes to curated TF signatures. The result is a single dominant regulatory axis per sample, providing mechanistic clarity without computational overhead.

Method Overview

  • Input: bulk or single‑cell RNA‑seq expression matrices and metadata defining two states.

  • Gene ranking: median‑based log2 fold change or other robust delta metrics.

  • Max‑delta selection: top N genes by absolute change (default N = 300).

  • Signature mapping: intersection with minimal TF signatures.

  • Axis scoring: per‑gene z‑scoring followed by mean signature expression.

  • Output: axis scores and dominant axis labels per sample.

Key Advantages

  • Mechanistic interpretability through TF axis activation.

  • Robustness to cohort heterogeneity.

  • Simplicity of deployment and reproducibility.

  • Extensibility to custom signatures or alternative scoring methods.

Practical Course‑of‑Action Guide

This deposit includes a practical guide designed to help users navigate Windows, PowerShell, and Python environments without relying on rigid step‑by‑step instructions. The guide outlines the sequence of decisions and actions needed to run DRA reliably:

  1. Establish a working directory.

  2. Confirm Python availability.

  3. Create a clean environment (venv or conda).

  4. Verify file paths and permissions.

  5. Run the pipeline on example data.

  6. Interpret axis scores and dominant axis labels.

  7. Scale up to real datasets.

  8. Optionally integrate with GeneXplain.

  9. Troubleshoot systematically.

  10. Maintain reproducibility practices.

This approach is resilient to differences in system configuration and avoids the pitfalls of overly rigid workflows.

Methods Summary

Core Algorithm

  • Compute per‑gene delta between states using median‑based log2 fold change.

  • Select top N genes by absolute delta.

  • Map selected genes to TF signatures.

  • Z‑score selected genes across samples.

  • Compute axis scores as mean z‑scores across signature genes.

  • Assign dominant axis per sample.

Parameter Guidance

  • topN: default 300; adjust for cohort size.

  • Delta metric: log2 fold change or robust alternatives.

  • Scoring: mean z‑score or more advanced methods (GSEA, regulon activity).

Implementation Notes

  • Uses an appropriate Python version with standard scientific libraries.

  • Containerization recommended for exact reproducibility.

  • Signature curation is intentionally minimal and transparent.

Provenance and Reproducibility

metadata.title: Legal Protection for Reog Ponorogo Folklore as an Intangible Cultural Heritage Under Copyright Law Number 28 of 2014 and the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage
metadata.description: This study aims to analyze the form of legal protection for Reog Ponorogo folklore as an intangible cultural heritage under Law Number 28 of 2014 concerning Copyright, and to examine the implementation of the principles of the 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) regarding the protection of the art form. The research method employed is a qualitative empirical-juridical approach using case study, phenomenological, and ethnographic methods through the examination of primary and secondary legal materials, as well as field investigations in Ponorogo Regency. The results indicate that the Ponorogo Regency Government has pursued preventive legal protection measures. These include periodic inventories, the standardization of dance core guidelines (pakem) in the form of reference books, the regeneration of artists through local-content-based formal school education, and the Copyright registration of the Bantarangin version with the Directorate General of Intellectual Property (DGIP) since 2004. Internationally, the Reog Ponorogo culture was officially inscribed onto the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list at the 19.COM session in 2024. Although the ICH Convention emphasizes non-executive and non-economic safeguarding to protect heritage from extinction within the public domain, the synchronization of national regulations specifically a dedicated Government Regulation (PP) concerning communal economic exploitation based on Copyright is absolutely required to mitigate foreign unilateral claims sustainably.

metadata.title: FUNDAMENTAL FOUNDATIONS OF HIGHER MATHEMATICS
metadata.description:
Mathematics provides the conceptual language through which patterns, structures, quantities, and relationships can be described with precision. It is fundamental not only to the mathematical sciences but also to engineering, computer science, economics, physics, and many other fields that rely on logical analysis and quantitative reasoning. A sound understanding of higher mathematics therefore requires more than familiarity with formulas. It requires the ability to interpret definitions, recognize mathematical structures, justify procedures, and communicate conclusions accurately. Fundamental Foundations of Higher Mathematics: Volume I has been prepared as a bachelor’s degree textbook for students beginning their systematic study of university-level mathematics. Its principal purpose is to establish a coherent foundation in linear algebra, vector algebra, analytic geometry, and the introductory concepts of mathematical analysis. The material is organized to support the gradual transition from computational methods to abstract mathematical reasoning. The volume begins with matrices and determinants, which provide an efficient framework for representing linear relationships and transformations. Matrix operations, determinant properties, inverse matrices, rank, and related structural concepts are developed together with their computational applications. The study of systems of linear equations extends these ideas by examining consistency, uniqueness, elimination methods, and
the interpretation of solutions through matrix structure. The treatment of vector algebra connects algebraic operations with geometric meaning. Vectors are introduced as mathematical objects representing magnitude and direction, followed by linear combinations, scalar and vector products, projections, and geometric applications. These concepts form the basis for the subsequent study of analytic geometry.
The chapters on analytic geometry examine geometric objects through coordinate, vector, and algebraic methods. Lines and curves in the plane are studied before the discussion is extended to points, lines, and planes in threedimensional space. Particular attention is given to the relationship between equations and the geometric objects they represent. The study of quadric surfaces further develops this relationship by analyzing second-degree surfaces, their standard forms, classifications, coordinate transformations, and geometric properties. The later part of the volume introduces the language and foundational ideas required for mathematical analysis. Sets, real numbers, intervals, bounds, supremum, infimum, and related concepts are presented as essential tools for rigorous reasoning. Functions are then examined through their domains, ranges, graphs, classifications, transformations, and qualitative properties. The final chapter develops sequences, limits, and continuity, thereby establishing the conceptual basis for the subsequent study of differential and integral calculus. Throughout the textbook, computational techniques are presented together with their mathematical meaning. Definitions are stated carefully, formulas
are accompanied by explanations of their notation and conditions, and procedures are developed in a logical sequence. Worked examples illustrate the application of general principles, while tables and diagrams clarify relationships that may be difficult to interpret from symbolic expressions alone. Chapter learning outcomes, summaries, and review exercises are included to support systematic study and self-assessment. A central principle of this textbook is that mathematical operations should not be performed mechanically or without attention to their assumptions. Students are encouraged to verify dimensions, domains, sign conditions, geometric interpretations, and theorem hypotheses before applying a formula. They are also expected to distinguish exact mathematical conclusions from numerical approximations and to present solutions in a clear, reproducible form. The textbook is suitable for classroom instruction, guided independent study, and review. Instructors may follow the chapters in their presented order or select topics according to the requirements of a particular academic program. The progression of the material is designed to help students develop both procedural competence and conceptual understanding. Exercises of varying
levels of difficulty may be used for classroom discussion, individual practice, homework, or examination preparation. 
Students are encouraged to read mathematical definitions actively, reproduce derivations independently, verify worked examples, and explain results in complete mathematical sentences. Progress in higher mathematics depends not only on obtaining correct answers but also on understanding why a method is valid, when it may be applied, and how its result should be interpreted. The authors hope that this volume will provide students with a reliable foundation for further study in calculus, linear algebra, differential equations, mathematical analysis, probability, numerical methods, and related disciplines. It is also hoped that the textbook will promote precision, logical discipline, intellectual independence, and an appreciation of the unity
between algebraic, geometric, and analytical methods. We express our appreciation to the educators, researchers, and authors whose work has contributed to the development and teaching of these subjects. We also acknowledge the students and colleagues whose questions and observations have helped emphasize the importance of clarity, consistency, and careful mathematical exposition. Despite every effort to ensure accuracy, constructive comments and recommendations concerning the content, organization, and presentation of the textbook will be welcomed and considered in future editions.

This dataset (version zen2025V01) provides population and human-capital projection
outputs for the five Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), re-based on a 2025 jump-off
population, covering 2025-2100 at five-year intervals. Results are generated with the
Multidimensional Demographic Modelling (MDM) workflow, the cohort-component machinery
used for the Wittgenstein Centre / SSP projections, and are disaggregated by region, sex,
five-year age group, and six levels of educational attainment. All files are provided in
open CSV format.

Each scenario is uploaded as a separate CSV file, allowing users to download only the
pathway they need. In addition to the projection outputs, the dataset includes a recode
dictionary and a file overview to support interpretation, together with a README
describing the structure and known caveats.

The projection files contain five-year interval estimates of population size, births,
deaths, immigration, and emigration by region, sex, age, and education. Variable
descriptions, value labels, and category mappings are provided in Recode dictionary.csv.

Note on SSP2: SSP2 is unchanged by the 2025 re-basing. The re-basing takes the SSP2
projection's 2025 population as the new jump-off state and applies the SSP1, SSP3, SSP4,
and SSP5 assumptions from 2025 onward. SSP2 projected from the earlier base year already
passes through exactly that state, so the 2025-based SSP2 and the original SSP2 describe
the same trajectory. All five scenarios therefore share an identical 2025 population of
approximately 8.15 billion, and the SSP2 file serves as the common reference pathway.

Notes for users: the files contain individual countries together with UN area, subregion,
and world aggregates in the same table. Filter on the region_level column before
aggregating, otherwise totals will be double-counted. Rows with agest = -5 are a newborn
accounting placeholder rather than a stock age group and should be excluded when computing
population stocks; a small number of terminal-period rows at that age carry negligible
negative values as a rounding artefact.

These are scenario outputs, not probabilistic forecasts. They should not be read as
predictions, and long-run country-level results for small territories warrant particular
caution.
metadata.method:
These projections are produced with the Multidimensional Demographic Modelling (MDM)
workflow, the multidimensional cohort-component model used for the Wittgenstein Centre
(WIC) population and human-capital projections (Lutz, Butz & KC, 2014; KC & Lutz, 2017).
Population is projected in five-year steps by country, sex, five-year age group, and six
levels of educational attainment (no education, some primary, primary, lower secondary,
upper secondary, post-secondary). Coverage is 200 countries and territories; UN area,
subregion, and world figures are aggregated from the country results.

Starting point. The scenarios build on the WIC2023 round of the SSP population and
human-capital projections (KC et al., 2024). WIC2023 uses 2020 as its reference year and
revised the treatment of fertility, mortality, education, and migration relative to earlier
rounds, including updated education-specific fertility estimates, country- and
region-specific education differentials in mortality, and, for the first time,
education-specific migration rates.

The 2025 re-basing. Rather than re-estimating a new empirical base year, the scenarios in
this dataset are re-anchored on the projected 2025 population by age, sex, and education
from the SSP2 pathway. That 2025 state becomes the common jump-off for all five SSPs, and
the SSP1, SSP3, SSP4, and SSP5 assumptions (O'Neill et al., 2017) on fertility, mortality,
educational attainment, and migration are applied from 2025 onward.

One consequence deserves emphasis: SSP2 is unchanged by the re-basing. The SSP2 pathway
projected from 2020 already passes through its own 2025 state, so the re-based SSP2 and the
original SSP2 describe the same trajectory. All five scenarios share an identical 2025
population of approximately 8.15 billion, and divergence between them emerges only after
2025. The SSP2 file therefore serves as the reference pathway for the set.

Scenario assumptions. Fertility and educational-attainment transitions follow the
SSP-specific assumptions of the corresponding WIC2023 pathway. Mortality follows the
low-mortality variant under SSP1 and SSP5 and the high-mortality variant under SSP3,
consistent with the SSP narratives (O'Neill et al., 2017). SSP4 combines the two by country
group: high-fertility countries take the high-mortality schedule, as in SSP3, while the
remaining countries follow the medium schedule used for SSP2. Migration is modelled with
age-specific emigration and immigration rates, with net international migration converging
to zero by 2060 and an additional correction applied to migration below age 15. All
scenarios carry the Ukraine displacement adjustment used in the WIC2023 baseline.

Outputs. Each file reports population stocks by cell together with the period flows that
generate them, births, deaths, immigration, and emigration, for every five-year period
from 2025 to 2100.

Status. These are scenario outputs, not probabilistic forecasts. They make a set of
internally consistent assumptions explicit and traceable; they are not predictions, and
long-run country-level results for small territories should be interpreted with care.

This repository provides the data, analysis code, numerical outputs, and documentation required to reproduce the center-eccentricity demonstration presented in the manuscript:

“Physics-Guided Scientific Discovery (PGSD): A Reference Architecture for Explainable Knowledge Generation in Mechanical Engineering.”

Version 1.1 supersedes version 1.0. It corrects the reference-sphere diameter from 24.9984 mm to 24.98484 mm and consequently updates the effective probe-center contact radius to:

R_e = 15.49242 mm.

The original CNC measurement files are preserved unchanged. The correction affects the contact-geometry constants, the constant-radius interpretation, and the calculated higher-order contact scale. It does not change the first-order LFH differential coefficient pair because those coefficients are estimated from the measured-coordinate columns and angular directions.

The demonstration uses two CNC touch-probing acquisitions of the reference sphere, denoted X0Y0 and LT_X0Y0, each containing 32 equatorial measurement points. A nominal relative offset of (-0.300, -0.300) mm was introduced through the CNC/G54 command between the two acquisitions.

The package includes:

  • the original CNC measurement files in CMM format;
  • normalized coordinate datasets;
  • Python scripts for Local Fourier Harmonic analysis and circle fitting;
  • numerical results corresponding to the manuscript;
  • files used to reproduce Figure 4;
  • documentation of the coordinate convention, units, sampling sequence, contact-geometry constants, and execution procedure;
  • a version history and correction note;
  • a package manifest and SHA-256 checksums.

The package reproduces the first-order LFH differential coefficient pair:

  • Delta a1 = -0.299865 mm
  • Delta b1 = -0.300743 mm

and the corresponding provisional inferred magnitude of 0.424695 mm. Using the corrected effective contact radius, the characteristic second-order contact scale is 2.90465 micrometres.

The nominal CNC/G54-commanded offset was not independently measured using an external calibrated displacement reference. Therefore, the numerical differences between the LFH estimate and the nominal command must not be interpreted as independently verified displacement errors. Only one acquisition was available for each state, and no complete uncertainty budget, within-state repeatability study, or multi-state validation was performed. The reported coefficient pair is consequently classified as a physically and operationally corroborated Candidate Signature, not as a validated or canonical Signature.

Changes from version 1.0

  • corrected the reference-sphere diameter to 24.98484 mm;
  • updated the effective contact radius to 15.49242 mm;
  • updated the higher-order contact-scale calculation to 2.90465 micrometres;
  • updated the analysis documentation, numerical metadata, and checksums;
  • preserved the original CMM measurement files;
  • confirmed that the first-order LFH differential coefficients and provisional inverse estimate remain unchanged.

This package supports Section 6 of the PGSD Foundation Preprint v1.2.

metadata.title: GravBathy-Diff dataset: paired SRTM15+ and multibeam bathymetry with SWOT-derived marine gravity fields for seafloor super-resolution
metadata.description:
This archive contains the complete dataset used to train and evaluate GravBathy-Diff, a gravity-conditioned diffusion model for 5x seafloor bathymetry super-resolution.
 
The dataset pairs two independently observed bathymetric products with co-registered marine gravity fields derived from SWOT wide-swath altimetry. The high-resolution reference is NCEI multibeam bathymetry at approximately 3 arc seconds (about 90 m); the low-resolution input is SRTM15+ at approximately 15 arc seconds (about 450 m). The low-resolution layer is the released SRTM15+ grid and was not produced by downsampling the reference, which distinguishes this archive from synthetic super-resolution benchmarks.
 
Contents:
 
- 44 large co-registered source tile groups (40 training, 4 testing) covering four ocean regions: the central Pacific, the northwestern Atlantic, the northeastern Atlantic and the western Pacific.
- 8,205 model-ready patches (7,078 training, 1,127 testing), each providing six co-registered layers: multibeam bathymetry (320x320), SRTM15+ bathymetry (64x64), the east and north components of the deflection of the vertical, the free-air gravity anomaly, and the vertical gravity gradient (all 64x64).
- tile_index.csv and patch_index.csv, which link every patch to its source tile and geographic bounding box and report per-patch depth statistics.
 
All files are single-band float32 GeoTIFFs in EPSG:4326. Depths are in metres, negative below sea level, with no normalisation applied. The training and test sets are split at the level of complete source tiles, so no test patch shares any pixel or neighbouring context with a training patch.
 
See README.md in the archive for the full data descriptor, including grid specification, naming conventions, provenance, processing steps and known caveats.

metadata.title: PREDICTIVE MAINTENANCE OF PRODUCTION EQUIPMENT USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE METHODS
metadata.description: The work provides a comprehensive analysis of modern approaches to predictive maintenance of production equipment using artificial intelligence methods. It examines the features of reactive, preventive, and predictive maintenance strategies, as well as the principles for building predictive maintenance systems. Modern machine learning methods are analyzed, including Random Forest, LSTM, GRU, Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, and autoencoders, highlighting their advantages, limitations, and suitability for tasks such as classifying equipment condition, predicting remaining equipment life, and detecting anomalies. The typical architecture of predictive maintenance systems has been summarized, and a comparative analysis of modern industrial predictive maintenance platforms has been carried out. Based on a review of the literature, an original qualitative comparison of machine learning methods and a generalized scheme of how predictive maintenance systems function have been developed. It was found that the effectiveness of such systems depends on a combination of quality data preparation, the choice of machine learning algorithms, and architectural decisions. The results obtained can be used as a methodological basis for designing intelligent predictive maintenance systems for production equipment in various industrial sectors.
